# Africa

# Central Africa

## Azande

Larken, P. M. 1926. “An Account of the Zande.” In Sudan Notes and Records, Vol. 9. 1926, Khartoum. [S.n.].

p.32a

“Nails of the hands are pared with a knife, and their surfaces sometimes scraped. Among the Vungara excessively long ones are occasionally seen, especially that of the little finger. Toe nails are not attended to.”

p.33-34

Cut hair is concealed usually, though by no means invariably, on account of the danger from magic, as are nail parings. But it is more important to conceal hair, as a shaved head being a sign of mourning, if it is left lying about, a death in the family may follow. Such a death may also occur if it is burnt. Therefore, it is advisable to conceal it.

## Barundi

Meyer, Hans, and Helmut Handzik. 1916. The Barundi: An Ethnological Study of German East Africa. 1916, Leipzig. Ott Spamer. p.12.

Aristocrats let the nail on the little finger grow to a length of 1 1/2 to 2 1/2 centimeters as a mark of their nobility and their freedom from manual labor.

## Mongo

Hulstaert, Gustave E., and Monika B. Vizedom. 1938. “Marriage among the Nkundu.” In MéIn-8, vol. 8. 1938, Bruxelles. Librairie Falk fils, Georges Van Campenhout, Successeur. p.458.

The helper crushes all of this to make a dish of food. While she cooks it over the fire, she shaves a little hair off the mother, plucks out one eyebrow, and cuts one of her nails. Then she does the same to the child.

## Eastern Africa

### Amhara

Messing, Simon D. (Simon David), and M. Lionel (Marvin Lionel) Bender. 1985. “Highland Plateau Amhara of Ethiopia.” In Ethnography Series. 1985, New Haven, Conn. Human Relations Area Files. p.275.

Nails are given little attention, except in the case of the bride, whose nails are trimmed, usually a day before the wedding, so that she will not be able to scratch the bridegroom when he has to use force to deflower her. Her nails are cut so short that not infrequently the skin is cut, and hot butter is applied, to heal them and also render the fingers caressingly smooth.

### Bagisu

Roscoe, John. 1924. The Bagesu and Other Tribes of the Uganda Protectorate: The Third Part of Hte Report of the Mackie Ethnological Expedition to Central Africa. 1924, Cambridge [Eng.]. The University Press. p.25-26.

When the midwife saw that there were twins, she might not remove the children from the spot where they were born before she had obtained the sanction of the medicine-man...

On the third day, the heads of the twins were shaved and their nails pared and then for seven months the father collected fowls, goats and promises of food for the ceremony of bringing the twins out for inspection.

### Banyoro

Roscoe, John, and - Mackie Ethnological Expedition To Central Africa. 1923. The Bakitara or Banyoro: The First Part of the Report of the Mackie Ethnological Expedition to Central Africa. 1923, Cambridge [Eng.]. The University Press.

p.121

The king's head was shaved and his nails pared by a special wife of the Bakwonga clan... The body was placed on a bedstead and kept from two to six days until everything was ready for the announcement of the king's death.

p.168

The teeth of the prince were handed to his nurse who had the other relics, such as the stump of the umbilical cord and the first teeth. She also kept his hair and nail-clippings, which had to be cut V-shaped and never broken. At death these were buried with the body.

p.180

Both men and women of the pastoral classes were careful to keep their bodies clean, and among the upper classes it was usual to have a daily bath, after which perfumed butter was rubbed on the body until no trace of grease was visible. The hair on the head was shaved off entirely every few weeks and the nails were kept short. Hair and nail-clippings had always to be deposited in some safe place where they were not likely to be found and used for casting spells on their owner.

p.258

When the first teeth were shed, they were given to the mother who placed them in a special basket and treasured them with other relics, such as the stump of the umbilical cord and, later, the teeth which were extracted at puberty. She also had to look after the hair and nail-cuttings of the child which, among the pastoral people, had to be thrown on a special place on the dung-heap, and among the agricultural people under a plantain-tree. Among the pastoral people it was the duty of a wife, mother, or sister to cut the hair and nails of a man or boy, but the serfs had no such rules.

Beattie, John. 1961. “Nyoro Mortuary Rites.” Uganda Journal Vol. 25 (2): 2. p.176

At the end of these four (or three) days, the mourners go into the high grass a little way from the house, and wash with a decoction of a plant called mubuza, 29 29 The symbolism here seems to depend on a pun; the idea is ‘to lose, get rid of, the death’ (okubuza orufu). shave one another's heads, pare their nails, and anoint themselves with oil...Some of the hair and nail clippings are collected and thrown on the grave, as also are the dry banana leaves on which the mourners have slept.

Nyakatura, J. W. (John W.), and Zebiya Kwamya Rigby. 1970. Aspects of Bunyoro Customs and Tradition. East African Literature Bureau. p.79.

The hair must not be combed or nails cut during the mourning period and are an outward sign of mourning. They are cut afterwards to show that life must go on somehow. .

Beattie, John. 1971. The Nyoro State. 1971, Oxford. Clarendon Press. p.115.

The dead king's body was laid out by special officials, and his nails and hair were cut by a woman of the Bakwonga clan.

Beattie, John. 1960. “Bunyoro, an African Kingdom.” In Case Studies in Cultural Anthropology. 1960, New York. Holt. p.27.

The second of the broad categories of ritual which I distinguished was that concerned with the acquisition, retention, and relinquishing of kingly power. Nyoro accession ceremonies are lengthy and complex...The accession ceremonies include washing, shaving, and nail-paring rites, anointment with a special oil and smearing with white chalk, ceremonial milk drinking, and animal sacrifice.

### Bilen

Munzinger, Werner, and Paul Anthony Moore. 1859. About the Customs and Laws of the Bogos. 1859, Winterthur. J. Wurster & comp. p.66.

Here, too, women are very fond of jewelry and make-up... Long nails are of good tone.

### Fur

Beaton, Arthur Charles. 1948. “The Fur.” Sudan Notes and Records Vol. 29: 1–39. p.30.

A man's brother will shave his head for him monthly, his wife will pluck the hair from his armpits and he will trim his own beard and moustache and shave his own pubic regions. Nails are cut with a knife and no ceremonial or magical customs attach to the destruction of the parings; henna staining is a foreign practice.

### Ganda

Roscoe, John. 1911. The Baganda: An Account of Their Native Customs and Beliefs. 1911, London. Macmillan and Co.

p.24.

A Cutting the hair and the nails. The King, his wives, and all members of the royal family had their nails cut into a V-shape, so that the point was in the centre; if any one else was detected cutting his nails in a V-shape, he was accused of trying to represent himself as connected with the royal family, and might be put to death for presumption. After cutting his nails a man would say, “I shall eat meat, before I need cut my nails again,” and this was supposed to bring him luck.

p.117.

During the time of mourning, the mourners were not allowed to shave their heads, nor to cut their nails, nor to wash, except to wash their hands for meals;

p.443.

A Nudity. A Cutting hair and nails...during mourning it was customary to leave both the hair and the nails to grow long, until the period of mourning ended. No person might cut his nails on his hands and his feet on the same day; had he done so, it would have been said that he wished to kill his parents. Royalty had their nails cut to a V-shaped point, but no commoner was permitted to imitate them in this respect; anyone who had done so would have been liable to punishment, and might even have been put to death. The nailparings of the King were preserved, sometimes also those of a chief, and were buried with him when he died, though no reason is given to account for the custom.

### Maasai

Merker, Meritz, and Frieda Schütze. 1910. The Masai: Ethnographic Monograph of an East African Semite People. 1910, Berlin. Dietrich Reimer (Ernst Vohsen). p.334.

The nails are cut with an ordinary two-edged knife. The two middle lower incisors are not broken out for everyone. Hair and nail cuttings are thrown away or hidden at some distance from the kraal, so that they will not fall into the hands of an evil sorcerer, who would be able to make from them sorcery leading to a sickness for their former wearer.


## Northern Africa

### Berbers of Morocco

Westermarck, Edward. 1926. Ritual and Belief in Morocco. 1926, London. Macmillan and Co. p.68.

An important preparation for the feast is the use of henna, which I have found among all the country people of whose customs I have obtained information, with the exception of the Rifians of Temsaman; and, as has been said above, henna is used not merely as a cosmetic but as a means of protection against evil influences.

Grown-up or married men abstain from it altogether (Hiaina, Andjra, Ait Sadden, Aglu), or only smear it on the palms of their hands or the tips of their fingers (At Ubahti), or dip the little finger of their right hand (Dukkala) or its nail (Ait Waryager) into it.

### Fellahin

Ayrout, Henry Habib, Hilary Wayment, and M. Taher Pasha. 1945. The Fellaheen. 1945, Cairo. R. Schindler. p.82.

The use of henna (lawsonia inermis) to dye the hair, hands, feet or perhaps only the nails, is a characteristically Egyptian affectation. It goes back to the Twentieth Dynasty, and Islam has encouraged it ( 37 ) 37. Vonderheyden: LE HENNÉ CHEZ LES MUSULMANS DE L'AFRIQUE DU NORD: JOURNAL DES AFRICANISTES, Paris, 1934, Vol. IV, pp. 55–61 and 179–202. . The application of henna is a delicate affair. A poultice, made with the powdered leaves, has to be applied hot and kept on from three to twenty-four hours according to quality. This produces a reddish-orange or brown colouring, which lasts about a fortnight.

### Tuareg

Lhote, Henri, and Mary-Alice Sipfle. 1944. “The Hoggar Tuareg.” In Bibliothèque Scientifique. 1944, Paris. Payot. p.117.

The Tuareg appreciate the long, narrow hands of people who do no manual labor. They do not take any particular care of them and are satisfied merely to cut their nails rather short. As they do for hair, they bury the scraps so that no one can take them.

## Southern Africa

### Ila

Smith, Edwin William and Dale, Andrew Murray, d. 1919. 1920. The Ila-Speaking Peoples of Northern Rhodesia: Vol. 1. 1920, London. MacMillan and Co. p.66.

The nails are never cut, but are allowed to grow till they break off. The possession of long nails has become a sign of wealth and position, for if a person has to work it inevitably happens that he breaks his nails; when you see a man with nails nearly an inch long you may readily conclude that he does no manual work, that is to say, he is a chief. Another motive assigned for the custom is expressed thus, balazanda kuambanya mala (“they want to use their nails to argue with”). It is common among the women, and not unknown among the men, to scratch and pinch each other in course of a dispute.

### Zulu

Berglund, Axel-Ivar. 1976. “Zulu Thought-Patterns and Symbolism.” In Studia Missionalia Upsaliensia. 1976, Uppsala. Swedish Institute of Missionary Research.

p.131.

Thirdly, associated with the brooding of the shades is abstention from cutting the hair and, sometimes, the paring of at least one nail, sometimes several. This is applicable to diviners who do not cut their hair or, if males, do not shave at all.

...

The diviner at eThelezini had a left-hand little-finger nail measuring about three centimeters in length. I suggested that the nail was a sign of his dignity. But he emphatically refuted this statement. “Do not confuse diviners and chiefs. Chiefs have it as a sign of not working. 13 13 Joest, Reise in Afrika im Jahre 1883, p. 482, describes Zulu dignitaries with a long finger-nail. But I for one, I work, doing the work of divination. (We had been talking of symbols of dignity and hence a discussion on long finger-nails.) This thing (he held out his finger nail) is the thing of brooding, like the hair. They are the same, the nail and the hair. If it (the nail) breaks, then surely I must beg pardon of them that own it (the shades). It is their thing of brooding.” Although a number of diviners do not have long fingernails, conservative and traditionalist diviners of standing will undoubtedly have at least one long finger nail. Usually it is on the left hand little finger, although other fingers may be chosen also. A diviner in the Msinga valley had three left-hand fingers with exceptionally long nails. Fig. 6. Diviner with uncut hair as a sign of the brooding of the shades. She wore three gall bladders from animals slaughtered in connection with her calling, training and coming out. The white tail hairs are of the beast killed on the occasion of her coming out. She associated them with “their owners”, i.e. the shades, with terminology similar to that used by the diviner in the uMhlatuse valley. 14 14 On long finger-nails see Lagercrantz, Contribution to the Ethnography of Africa, pp. 138–144.

p.132.

Because the hair, and where applicable also the nails, are intimately connected with life and health, imphilo, shaving the hair and paring the nails is a symbol of a new start in life, the climax of the former having been sanctioned by the brooding of the shades. When a child is born, it is shaved because it ceases to be a foetus and becomes an infant as a married woman who becomes a widow ceases to be a wife and commences the life of a widow. These associations of crisis are sanctioned by the very close and intimate nearness of the shades characterised by their brooding. When this particular life comes to an end under their brooding, a new life commences in which their presence is not that of brooding but rather of presence at some distance. Hence the shaving. An informant at Ekuthuleni said: “When a widow shaves, it is a sign that she is no longer inkosikazi. She now becomes a widow. She is like the bride (we spoke of) who leaves her homestead and goes to the home of her husband. She shaves to show that she is leaving behind her ubunthombi (maidenhood). That is why she shaves.”

Callaway, Henry. 1868. Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words, with a Translation into English, and Notes. 1868, Springvale, South Africa; Pietermaritzburg, South Africa; London. John A. Blair; Davis and Sons; Trübner and Co. p.190.

They said, “Turn up the millstone, and grind the boiled corn.” She replied, “I cannot grind, I am the king's child. Look here,”—showing them her hands, for her nails were very long. 34 34 Chiefs and great men allow their nails to grow long; such long nails are regarded as honourable. But women are not allowed to have long nails, as they would interfere with their work. Umk x akaza being the chief's child, has allowed her nails to grow. Cutting the nails is a reproof for her idleness and uselessness. One of the leaves took a knife and said, “Hand hither your hand to me.” It cut off the nails with the knife, and said, “Now grind.” Umk x akaza said, “I cannot grind; I am the king's child.” The leaves said, “We already knew that you could not grind, and that you were the king's child.”

Krige, Eileen Jensen. 1965. The Social System of the Zulus. 1965, Pietermaritzburg. Shuter & Shooter. p.374.

Certain ornaments are indications of rank, and in some cases ordinary people may not use them; only kings and great men wear the skin of the large grey baboon. 1 1 Callaway, Nursery Tales, p. 117. Men of standing used to allow their nails to grow long; such nails were regarded as honourable, and women were not allowed to have them.

## Western Africa

### Akan

Sarpong, Peter. 1977. Girls’ Nubility Rites in Ashanti. 1977, Tema, Ghana. Ghana Pub. Corp.

p.28.

Dressing the Girl —Immediately after the shaving, an old woman cuts the finger-nails and toe-nails of the girl. It is known that the woman, wanting to avenge herself for any wrongs the girl may have done her, may deliberately inflict little wounds on the tips of the girl's fingers so that she may feel pain when she is eating or bathing. The widespread nature of this practice, however, appears to justify considering it as part of the ceremony, reminiscent of the initiatory physical operations among some peoples, and not just as the outcome of vindictiveness. It would then be meant to give her a foretaste of the later (painful) experiences that are the lot of a wife and mother. 19 19 This interpretation, in fact, was given me at Konongo.

p.63.

The girl's nails are cut so that she may look as neat as a respectable Ashanti woman should. The shiny and greasy shea-butter (according to the Ashanti) adds to the beauty of a woman. There is no doubt, therefore, that the way the girl is dressed up distinctly marks her out as an adult woman, with all the characteristics of an Ashanti woman.

### Hausa

Rattray, R. S. (Robert Sutherland), and R.R. (Robert Ranulph) Marett. 1913. Hausa Folk Lore: Customs, Proverbs, Etc. In Two Volumes. 1913, Oxford, England. The Clarendon Press. [vol.2] p. 308.

Lal[unknown]e . A decoction of the leaves of the Lawsonia inermis . Henna, used by the Hausas to stain the nails; in the case of a bride the whole feet are stained up to the ankles, the hands to the wrists.

Karo, Baba of, and Mary Felice Smith. 1954. Baba of Karo, a Woman of the Muslim Hausa. 1954, London. Farber and Farber. p.266.

Unfortunately it was not established by field-enquiries whether or not a girl’s hands and feet are ever stained with henna before she is married, and the ritual significance of henna in this context is thus not as clear as it should be. In general, married women stain their hands and feet by covering them with a paste of dried ground henna-leaves, tied on with more leaves and old pieces of cloth, the whole being left overnight. When it is removed in the morning the skin is a reddish-brown colour and the nails are red. This is done before any festive occasions or visits to friends or relatives, and looks more attractive than it sounds.

Hill, Polly. 1972. Rural Hausa: A Village and Setting. 1972, Cambridge, England. University Press. p.267.

Henna - lalle (Lawsonia inermis) . The dried leaves of this cultivated perennial shrub (Egyptian privet), which may flourish for many years, are pounded and made into a paste which, usually by bandaging (but sometimes by immersing the arm in a cylindrical gourd), is applied as a reddening cosmetic to women’s hands, nails, arms, legs, feet, etc., both in everyday life and in marriage and childbirth rituals.

### Nupe

Forde, Cyril Daryll. 1955. “The Nupe.” 1955, London. Preprint, International African Institute. p.29.

Barber-doctors cut hair for men, women, and children; shave the head and cut the tribal marks of new-born babies at the naming ceremony and cut toe and finger nails.

### Wolof

Gamble, David P. 1957. “The Wolof of Senegambia: Together with Notes on the Lebu and the Serer.” In Ethnographic Survey of Africa: Western Africa. 1957, London. International African Institute. p.73.

Eyebrows are blackened—in the latest style the brow is continued in a curve down to the cheekbone—and a blue line is marked under the lower eyelids by kohl or antimony, making the eyes appear larger. The lower lips of the women, and sometimes the gums are tattooed blue, which is highly effective against their black skins. Palms of hands, soles of the feet, and nails are stained with henna.

# Asia

## Central Asia

### Pashtun

Ahmed, Akbar S. 1980. “Pukhtun Economy and Society: Traditional Structure and Economic Development in a Tribal Society.” In International Library of Anthropology. 1980, London; Boston. Routledge & Kegan Paul.

p.104.
The barber cuts the hair and finger-nails of males although nail-cutters are becoming common. Women cut their own hair and use blades to cut their nails.

p.175.

The barber's functions are as manifold as they are versatile. He shaves the face and head of his clients and clips their nails, circumcises their male offspring, carries invitations during the rites de passage, registers and records money paid during the rites ( nindara ) and may even substitute as the cook if the professional kulal is not available during the rites. The nai 's wife is called a naiganra but she does not perform the duties of her husband. Mohmand women cut their own hair and clip their own nails.

### Tibetans

Macdonald, David. 1929. The Land of the Lama: A Description of a Country of Contrasts & of Its Cheerful, Happy-Go-Lucky People of Hardy Nature & Curious Customs; Their Religion, Ways of Living, Trade & Social Life. 1929, London. Seeley, Service & Co., Ltd. p.158.

Like the Chinese, the nobles of Tibet think it a sign of rank and breeding to allow the finger-nails to grow long, though they do not carry the practice to such an extent as the Celestials, an inch being about the average. The long nail demonstrates the high rank of its wearer and his non-performance of any manual labour.

Waddell, L. A. (Laurence Austine). 1895. The Buddhism of Tibet: Or Lamaism; with Its Mystic Cults, Symbolism and Mythology, and in Its Relation to Indian Buddhism. 1895, London. W.H. Allen & Co. Ltd. p.179.

The initiation into the Tāntrik Buddhist priesthood of the Vajrācāryas is detailed below in a foot-note... Then be causes the aspirant to perform his ablutions, after which he makes pújā to the hands of the barber in the name of Visvakarma, and then causes the barber to shave all the hair, save the forelock, off the aspirant's head. Then the paternal or maternal aunt of the aspirant takes the vessel of mixed metal above noted and collects the hair into it. The aspirant is now bathed again and his nails pared, when the above party puts the parings into the pot with the hair. ”

### Uyghur

Bellér-Hann, Ildikó. 2004. “Hair-Raising Stories: The Trickster in Uyghur Oral Tradition.” Asian Anthropology Vol. 3: 13–38. p.28.

Magical symbolism attached both to hair and to nails, regarded as living extensions of the body, explains the numerous prescriptions and prohibitions associated with them. It was considered potentially dangerous to leave hair and fingernails lying on the floor or ground. Both had to be dug or preserved somewhere safe to prevent bad luck or calamity ( Prov. 464.38V ), a general rule still widely observed in many parts of Central Asia.

## East Asia

### Korea

Moose, J. Robert. 1911. Village Life in Korea. 1911, Nashville. M.E. Church. p.105.

“Our gentleman is very particular about his appearance. If he can afford it, he always dresses nicely and is usually clean. Clothed in his spotless robes of white or in his skyblue silk, of a texture much like that of a spider's web, his appearance is dainty, not to say ‘dandy.’ His feet and hands are small and trim, his hands soft, and the nails on the little fingers allowed to grow long as a sign that he does no manual labor...”

Knez, Eugene Irving. 1970. Sam Jong Dong: A South Korean Village. University Microfilms. p.101.

(8) Fifth day of the fifth moon is known as dan-oh and is thought as principally a women's holiday... Younger women and girls paint their finger nails red with pong-sun-wha (balsam flower juice).

### Okinawans

Pitts, F. R., William P. Lebra, and Wayne P. Suttles. 1955. “Post-War Okinawa.” In Scientific Investigations in the Ryukyu Islands. 1955, Washington D.C. National Research Council, Pacific Science Board. p.148.

In care of the body, the Okinawans are among the cleanlier of the world's peoples. They bathe frequently, keep their nails clean by constant trimming, their teeth clean by prolonged morning brushing, and their hair neatly cut or dressed.

Hall, Basil. 1840. Narrative of a Voyage to Java, China, and the Great Loo-Choo Island. 1840, London. E. Moxon. p.40.

... but the nails of his left hand being about an inch and a half long, he found it not so easy a matter. He seemed to look upon gloves as very odd articles of dress, and, laughing heartily, held them up to the view of the other chiefs. This disagreeable fashion of allowing the nails to grow is a clumsy device borrowed from the Chinese, amongst whom it is considered a distinctive mark of riches, implying that the wearer is not reduced to manual labour, which under such circumstances would be impossible. The occasion furnishes one example out of many which we saw every day of the force of habit in rendering us blind to our own absurdities. These natives laughed heartily at the oddity of such a curious contrivance as a glove; but none of them could be made to understand why it was ridiculous to allow the mails to grow an inch or two beyond the finger-ends.

### Andamans

1. 7. White clay, used mixed with water, for ornamental painting of the person and of various articles, e.g. , bows, baskets, buckets, trays, &c.: the work is done by women: when painting their relatives they spare no pains in executing neat designs with their finger-nails.

### Badaga

Hockings, Paul. 1980. Sex and Disease in a Mountain Community. 1980, Sahibabad, Distt. Ghaziabad. Vikas Publishing Pvt Ltd. p.61.

3.12. A girl's first seclusion is for no fixed period. She can re-enter her home only on a Monday, Wednesday or Friday, but it must be either the first day after the new moon or else whichever of these three days falls most closely before the full moon. Although this is the Badaga custom, today one out of five girls would instead go to the nearest town and, in Tamilian fashion, consult an astrologer as to the most auspicious day for re-entering the house. On that day she bathes outside the house, puts on a set of totally new clothes, and cuts her nails with a small knife.

### Bengali

Östör, Ákos. 1980. The Play of the Gods: Locality, Ideology, Structure, and Time in the Festivals of a Bengali Town. 1980, Chicago. University of Chicago Press.

p.48.

After the different deities' pūjās, the ritual bathing begins... and appropriate gestures with a piece of wood represent the cutting of the goddess's nails.

p.143.

Certain jāti functions are to be noted. Barber and Brāhma are the most important specialists. The barber and the agradhānī Brāhma share certain duties in other contexts. The barber's presence is necessary for a number of life-cycle rites such as the upanayan (the bestowing of the sacred thread), wedding, and śrāddha (funerary ceremony). In these rites also, the barber's action of shaving and of paring nails marks the altered status of the person.

Fruzzetti, Lina M. 1992. Conch Shell Bangles, Iron Bangles: An Analysis of Women, Marriage, and Ritual in Bengal. University Microfilms.

p.152.

The dabi mugla concerns the female Barber's kit. Women participating in all the rituals have to be purified by having their nails cut and alta (red lac) applied to their feet by the Napit woman. The Napit is also sent to bring the women needed for the rites to the bride's house, so that all may go through the kamano (the purifying) together.

p.156.

The process of kamano is simple. The Napit always starts with the nails of the hand, left to right, going on to the feet in the same manner. Even if the nails need no cutting she touches them with her knife to accomplish the purification.

Fruzzetti, Lina M. 1982. The Gift of a Virgin: Women, Marriage, and Ritual in a Bengali Society. 1982, New Brunswick, N.J. Rutgers University Press.

p.48-49.

The dābi mugla is the blessing of the Nāpit's (barber's) shaving kit, which precedes the barber's participation in the rituals. Women participating in all the rituals have to be purified by having their nails cut and āltā (red lac) applied to their feet by the Nāpit woman. 15 15. Menstruating women cannot, however, participate in any of the rites.

...

The barbers have the most important caste function in the muglas and the barber's paona is always more than that of the Dom or Kāmāno: a woman barber helps purify the women. midwife. Kāmāno is a significant component of all life cycle rites, especially those most polluting, the actions surrounding death. In ritual contexts the Nāpit is a purifier; her touch will not pollute higher castes. The women can take the purifying bath before the Nāpit clips their nails. Doing her purifying work, the Nāpit woman faces south and uses a small blade, cotton dipped in āltā, and a stone to scrape the soles of the feet.

The process of kāmāno is simple. The Nāpit always starts with the nails of the hand, left to right, going on to the feet in the same manner. Even if the nails need no cutting she touches them with her knife for purification.

When hair and nails of the baby are cut for the first time, a good day must be chosen for this. It must not in any case take place on Kakoenia (14th day); also not when the field is planted or at the time of the harvest. Before one starts cutting, the child’s crown and forehead are spit upon ( rasoepa ) with finely chewed wild cinnamon ( pakanangi ); the little nails are pressed into a piece of curcuma or ginger, or they are rubbed with it. Then with a sliver of bamboo ( djimoejoe ) one cuts off some hair and scrapes the nails with it; after that the work may be continued with an iron knife, after this has been counted off from 1 -- 7. If iron were used immediately, the child would become a crosspatch ( taoe masii ). Nowadays scissors are used for this. One must let the hair on the crown stand, “so that the tanoana will have a support ( pangkekeninja ).” If father or mother do not cut the hair and nails of their child themselves, the one who does it must receive a reward, “so that the child’s tanoana will be cool.” Sometimes this reward is a resin torch, “so that the person will not become blind.” Some children, it is said, become thin after the cutting of their hair and nails. This comes about because their tanoana has gone away with the hair; it must then be enticed back with rice and egg.

## Central Mexico

### Nahua

Lewis, Oscar. 1951. Life in a Mexican Village: Tepoztlán Restudied. 1951, Urbana. University of Illinois Press. p.373.

Children are, for the most part, not hurried in their development. A healthy child is expected to walk at about one year and to talk at about two years. If the child does not walk by that time, some parents rub his leg and calf muscles with earth warmed by the sun, to remove the “cold” from his legs. More acculturated women may help their children learn to walk by placing a sash under the arms for support or by putting a toy before them. Children are only mildly encouraged to speak, by repeating words to them. There is little correction of childlike errors in speech, such as substituting “y” for “r” or omitting “s,” or misplacing syllables. so that errors persist until the child is five or six years of age. If a child cannot speak by the time he is three or four, a church key may be borrowed and turned in the child's mouth to “unlock” it. It is believed by many that the fingernails of a child should not be cut until he begins to speak, because the palate will fall and the child will be mute. To prevent children from scratching themselves with their long nails, some mothers put little mittens on their hands. When teeth are late in coming, the gums may be rubbed with a grasshopper's leg until the gums bleed. This is an old practice and is no longer known by many of the younger people. It is also believed that a child's hair should not be cut before one year, or the child will be come ill.

The use of black henna ( saumar ) for the soles of the feet and hands, and red henna ( hinna ) for the tips of the fingers and toes is universal among hadhar townswomen. The Badawin girls use only red henna and then only to decorate their hands, finger nails and toe nails. They do not decorate the rest of their feet. Usually the henna is applied three times, so as to get the right shade. The henna is powdered and mixed with water till a fairly liquid paste is made. It is then applied very thickly and carefully, with a wooden stick, on the hands or feet in accordance with the pattern desired. It is then allowed to dry quickly in front of a fire until the paste cracks and falls or is picked off. This is done three times, or four if a very dark colour is required.

On the evening before the festival, the Shaikh of Kuwait, having taken the necessary expert advice, gives out that the following morning is to be celebrated as 'Id, and great is the rejoicing, especially if it happens to be the 'Id that follows the long weary Fast of Ramadhán, for the end of this painful period, this difficult and exhausting penance, has come at last. For a whole fortnight beforehand women have been sewing and getting ready their multi-coloured frocks for the great occasion, and husbands and masters have been doling out kiswahs (new clothes) to their wives, dear ones, slaves and servants. Happiness is in the air, and all is pleasure and excitement as in the last days before our Christmas. Not the least important of the women's and children's duties at this period is the washing of their hair, bathing of their bodies, and the placing of henna on their hands and feet. This usually, in Kuwait, takes the form of red henna for finger and toe nails, and black henna on the palms of hands in different patterns, as well as on the feet. The actual method for applying henna and the patterns most favoured are described in Chapter IX.

It is important to choose a favorable day for cutting one's nails. If one cuts them on Saturday, one will have to pay one debts; if on Monday, one will grow rich; if on Thursday, one will lose a child; if on Friday, it will be a pious work (H.). Two verse proverbs sum up these recommendations: “Shave your head and cut your nails on the least unfavorable day possible. —Do not shave or cut 275 your nails on Sunday, Satur day or Tuesday.” Wednesday (during the day) is particularly favorable for cutting nails and hair (as well as for bathing).

If you clasp your hands together by folding your fingers over the backs of your hands, you will create difficulties for yourself in the future (“a knot will be tied in your affairs” gere be-kares mi-ofte). If you crack your knuckles, you will grow poor. White spots on the fingernails are a sign of new clothes ( 2 2. Might this be because tailors and seamstresses often have such white spots on their nails? ). If you cut a fingernail on one hand and do not cut the corresponding nail on the other, a dog will attack you (H.). Anyone who can cut the nails of his right hand with his left hand thereby shows that he is able to earn a living (H.). Throwing nails on the ground after they have been cut will bring discord or poverty (when they are trampled underfoot). If you kneel on one knee only and hold the other knee in your arms against your breast, you will grow poor. Squatting down will bring misfortune (H.). The same is true of urinating against a wall. Urinating in the basin of the hammam will make you forgetful or, according to others, will cause blindness (H.). One should never urinate either facing or turning one's back to Mecca or to the sun. If anyone sleeps on his stomach with the soles of his feet in the air, his father will die.

The paste is applied and, in the case of hands, feet, and nails, is left on for an hour. Long finger-nails should be avoided, since they furnish places of retreat for satans, and particular times for paring the nails are recognized. Thursday is a good day because he who cuts his nails on Thursday will never have sore eyes. Friday is also a good day, and if one desires the merit of doing this act on both days, he may leave one finger until Friday. If the nails grow rapidly and become too long from one Thursday to another, he may cut them on Monday. A man who did not adhere to these beliefs was cutting his nails on Wednesday, and his wife was alarmed at the prospect of some misfortune coming to them as the result of his carelessness and implored him to cut his nails only on Fridays and Mondays.

The order in which the nails should be trimmed is also specified. One should begin with the little finger of the left hand and end with the little finger of the right. If he must cut his nails on Wednesday, he may do so in safety by reversing the order!3

There is merit in its use, and often the hands and the feet are dyed with it, and sometimes it is rubbed on the entire body. p.134.

The henna plant is cultivated throughout India on account of its leaves, which yield the henna dye, and as a garden hedge plant. They are sold in the shops in two forms: (1) the broken leaves, and (2) the leaves called “Rangh” reduced to fine powder and mixed with a small quantity of mustard oil. The principal value is as an article of the toilet, for staining the finger nails, hands, and feet a dull orange color, and for dyeing the hair bright red. The use of henna as a cosmetic dates from very ancient times; it is practiced by Mohammedan women, and has become a vogue in Europe. Staining the finger nails with henna to make them resemble hazelnuts is called “funduq bastan.” Henna is also used as an external application for skin diseases, blind boils, and leprosy.—It is painted on the pubic region for stoppage of bladder (H.F.). The seeds contain about 10 per cent of fixed oil.

Hegland, Mary Elaine. 2004. “Iranians.” 2004, New York. Preprint, Kluwer Academic Plenum Publishers. p.519.

Iranian men wore a form of trousers, and women wore long skirts over loose trousers and a scarf, although men often also wore ethnic or regional hats. Affluent men could afford to veil and seclude their womenfolk at home, thus demonstrating their status. However, hardworking tribal and peasant women did not wear veils. Reza Shah Pahlavi forcibly removed women's veils—policemen tore off their scarves and veils—to symbolize Iranian modernity and westernization. He encouraged Western dress. Men took on Western clothing: trousers, suit jackets, ties, and hats. Women more often retained ethnic, tribal, or regional dress. Men wear their hair shorter and might have beards and mustaches. As infants and toddlers, mothers dressed girls and boys similarly in homemade shirts and pants, and only began to put dresses or skirted pullovers on girls, rather than boys' shorter pullovers, after the age of 2 or 3. People believe that girls should cover their hair by the age of 7, although girls might beg for a scarf or veil before then. At an early age, girls are expected to stay at home and not roam around the neighborhood with friends, as boys do. Use of make-up visibly marked the transformation of a girl to a married woman. Particularly during the time of Mohammad Reza Shah, middle- and upper-class urban women took to Western fashions, make-up, nail polish, and beauty shop hair care. In the 1960s and 1970s, girls wore uniforms to school, and generally teachers did not wear veils. Upper- and middle-class women, especially professionals, often did not wear veils except when attending religious gatherings.

They could enter into a covenant of intermarriage with the city of Shechem only if its males underwent the operation. It was a minor thing, they must have explained convincingly, in fact not much more than the paring of a nail. It also would have the advantage for the Shechemites to imprint into their flesh the sign of the noble nomadic status and would thus elevate them above the other townsfolk of the country, the Canaanites and Perizzites.

Within the village aristocracy this form of beauty culture is gradually becoming engaged in a struggle with European-American nail varnish which, like the henna, can be purchased in the saq and has also found its way to the villages. Nail varnish of whatever tint serves to emphasize the whiteness of the skin. The henna dye hides it. Use of them both results in a most unfortunate meeting between East and West, particularly when the henna dye gradually fades without at any time appearing unsightly, whilst the nail varnish peels off, as varnish remover is not apparently indulged in, giving a very slovenly effect.

Masters, William Murray. 1953. Rowanduz: A Kurdish Administrative and Mercantile Center. 1953, [S.L.]. [S.n.].

p.154.

A Kurdish townsman usually washes his hands and face at least once or twice each day. One of the ceremonials of a formal banquet involves cleansing. In entering to dine, certain persons, servants or children, pour water from a metal ewer above a basin over the hands of the guest, furnishing him soap and a towel. Each guest goes through this ritual before going to the table, in groups of two or three. It is repeated a second time when the meal is at an end. According to the direction of the Prophet, the Euslim worshipper must perform the “lesser ablution” ( Wudhu ), washing face, hands, and feet, before each of the five daily prayers. Because an observably large proportion of the populace, with no respect to social status, does not pray five times each day, it is difficult to form any idea of adherence. Similarly, the “greater ablution” ( ghusl ), a complete cleansing of the body, must be undertaken by Muslims after major pollutions, of which the commonest is sexual intercourse. An individual so concerned is nijis , “defiled” or “filthy,” a violent term of abuse, until bathed, and requiring of a husband the number of baths he has taken in a given period is tantamount to asking how many times he has gone to his wife. It is thus almost impossible, outside of direct observation, to obtain anything other than hearsay on the bathing habits of married people. Nevertheless, it can be seen that most townsmen bathe in the summer at least once or twice each week. The nails are cut with a knife, and cleaned with the same instrument. The attention paid to the parings will be noted later.

p.157.

Because the ablutions before prayers, with some reservation, apply to Muslims of both sexes, it is equally difficult to obtain an exact idea of the bathing habits of the townswomen. Unmarried girls are supposed to wash themselves completely twice or three times each week during the summer and once or twice each fortnight in colder weather. All of the hair of a woman's body must be removed: the pubic hair with a razor, that under the arms with the fingers, and the rest with a depilatory concocted of sugar and gum arabic. In addition, the ankles and feet are rubbed with a small piece of black stone. Both men and women clean the teeth with their fingers, pieces of rag, or European toothbrushes. The hair of a woman's head, on the other hand, is almost never cut or trimmed, and its length and richness are thought to be outstanding attributes of feminine beauty. Whenever two women quarrel, one often cries out “your hair will be cut,” a promise of great catastrophe for her opponent. At an early age, a girl begins to wear a number of braids, and, save when undone in the bath, this type of coiffure is retained until death. The number of braids varies, and is usually about ten. The hair is regularly stained a reddish colour with henna whose use, in addition to being purely customary, is said “to fortify the scalp.” In some houses, kuhl , a finely powdered sulphide of antimony moistened with water, is applied to blacken the edges of the eye. European cosmetics and perfumes appear in most of the wealthier homes, and younger women paint their lips and nails. Reddening the hands and feet with henna, a custom for both sexes at a wedding, is not an everyday practice. The so-called “Baghdad boil,” reported to be caused by larvae laid by a type of fly in the skin, usually of the face, is the bane of women in cities such as Baghdad or Mosul because of its hideous scar. It is not found in this area, nor is the technique used to prevent it from occurring on the countenance, artificial infection of the ankle or calf of a child. For menstruation clean pieces of rag are used as towels, and sexual intercourse is prohibited during the period. The cloths are commonly washed and reused. Tattooing is denied by most men to be done by women of the town, but it is possible to observe daily female residents of the lower classes with blue dots or marks inscribed on their faces. These are either transient servants or migrants from the villages where the use of tattooing is frequent. In the absence of investigation, the function of village tattooing in this area is not precisely known, but it appears that it has no tribal or territorial significance, and is either decorative, magical, or both.

p.159.

The toilet of children does not differ greatly from that of adults, and girls of wealthier homes use cosmetics in imitation of their mothers, just as the older boys remain unshaven in hopes of growing a moustache. For six months after birth, the nails of a baby must not be cut, and an infant's hair is trimmed for the first time at about the age of one year. At four or five the boys are ciroumoized, but the accompanying ceremony, as well as the operation itself, will be found described in a later section. The ear lobes of the girls can be pierced at any time in their early years, but cutting a nostril for the khizam or nose-ring is only to be seen in the villages.

p.161.

It has been seen that the townspeople have little regard for intoxicants, nor do they make use of drugs such as the opium of Iran to the east or the hashish of Lebanon and Syria to the west. If there are excesses among the natives of Rowanduz, they are only tea-drinking and smoking, the first of which has been discussed. Cigarettes are the most popular mode of consuming tobacco, and have several varieties. From the merchants British cigarettes and those made in the factories of Baghdad may be obtained. The officials and officers habitually use these, and they are usually offered to guests in wealthy homes or to visitors to a shop in the bazar . Most of the populace, however, smoke those prepared from local leaf in the houses by the women. These are made in great quantity by filling manufactured paper tubes, about four inches in length, and folding down the paper remaining at one end. A number of persons possess small Austrian cigarette-rollers, devices which can be carried on the person enclosing a certain amount of tobacco and a book of papers. Factory-made cigarettes are kept in their pasteboard boxes, and Baghdadis, some of the government personnel, have nowadays the habit, probably ephemeral, of letting the nail of the little finger on the left hand grow long with which to slit open the package. The longer domestic product is typically carried in a silvered metal box, resembling a covered soap-dish, imported from abroad. A number of persons use heavy cigarette holders of wood or imported beroid, out of proportion to the cigarette in thickness. In Ottoman times, many had pipes with long stems, two or three feet in length, but they have largely disappeared. It is still possible to buy pottery bowls in the bazar to which a drilled wooden shaft can be attached as a stem, but they are not popular. The water-pipe is not remembered as ever having had much use in the area. A smaller pipe survives among the villagers and men of the lower class, a stubby form in baked clay of curious design with an overall length of about five inches and the height of the bowl, two or three. One product of the area is a long wooden cigarette holder, cut from the thin branch of a cherry tree and laboriously drilled, but it has little more than curiosity value for the local people. European cigarette lighters are in great demand, and together with the dagger and the rosary form an important part in every adult male's ensemble. There are several varieties of these, and are Austrian in derivation. Several craftsmen in the town use flint and steel to light their pipes, but this is relatively rare, a survival among the poor and thrifty. Both men and women smoke, the latter as much as their husbands, and there is no restriction on youngsters. Children usually avoid tobacco as a matter of physical distaste, not because of any prohibition laid upon them. During the fasting hours of Ramadan it is considered impolite, if not impious, to smoke on the streets, although tobacco, of course, has no mention in the Quren.

p.259.

At the same time, they begin to wear clothing differentiating the sexes, shirts and trousers for the boys, dresses and undertrousers for the girls. The elder children teach them to avoid exposure of the sexual organs in public. Toilet training begins early, at five or six months, by the repetition of a nonsense word which signifies evacuation and is accompanied by the initial use of a pot. Gradually utilization of the latrine and its ewer of water is learned. After two or three years the mother and others of the family begin to punish a child who soils himself. For six months after birth the nails of a baby may not be cut, and the hair of a boy is clipped for the first time at the age of one year. The hair of the girls is stained with henna, and, when it has attained sufficient length, is braided. A girl's ear-lobes are pierced during her early childhood.

Garbarino, Merwyn S. 1989. Economic Development and the Decision-Making Process on Big Cypress Indian Reservation, Florida. University Microfilms. p.48.

Shortly after mother and baby return from the hospital, the baby's ears are pierced if it is a girl. Boys no longer have their ears pierced, but there are a number of men who had it done when they were infants. The umbilical cord is allowed to drop off, and most mothers till bury it in a shady spot although no informant could remember the reason behind this practice. After four moons have passed, the baby has his hair and nails cut, and these clippings are saved to give to the child when he is grown. The origins and meaning of this practice too have been forgotten. One woman said she thought it was “just like the white people do, like save the baby's shoes.” Sometimes a baby garment or two is added to this collection. After the hair cutting ceremony, most babies and mothers have a ritual cold water bath, and then it is considered proper for the mother to sleep with the father again. Traditionally during these four months, the mother and baby lived together in a separate chickee. An old medicine woman, a specialist in female ills, would sing songs to make the baby and mother strong. These songs used to be sung Just after the mid-wife delivered the baby, and today these songs are still often sung, but after the mother returns from the hospital. The baby's cradle is still the traditional hammock of sturdy white cloth suspended from the rafters of the chickee.

### Nuu-chah-nulth

Burning the flesh is also resorted to for other purposes. Boys will apply moxas made of dried and partially charred pitch, to the back of the thumbs from the nail to the wrist. When the sores heal, they leave scars or callous spots, which are supposed not only to keep the bow-strings from hurting the hand, but to give a steadiness of aim, so that they can throw their arrows with more precision. I have seen school-boys sit down of an evening by the fire and amuse themselves in this manner, holding out their hands with the burning pitch singing into the flesh, and showing their bravery by the amount of pain they could bear. I usually found, however, that they were very willing for me to dress their hands with salve whenever they had attempted this performance. Blood-letting is not practised according to our methods, but in case of bruises when there is swelling and much pain, they scarify the skin by cutting longitudinal and transverse gashes just deep enough to make the blood flow by keeping the part moistened with water. Cauterizing the flesh is, however, the favorite and most generally practised remedy for all internal complaints, and answers with the Indian the double purpose of blisters and bleeding.

### Quinault

Olson, Ronald L. (Ronald Leroy). 1936. “The Quinault Indians.” In University of Washington Publications in Anthropology, No. 1, v. 6. no. 1. 1936, Seattle, Wash. The University of Washington. p.60.

After puberty both young and old of both sexes kept the eyebrows trimmed to a thin curved line. Men removed all traces of beard. The straggling hair of the head was also pulled out. The nails or fingers dipped in ashes might be employed, but it was more common to pluck with tweezers made of a split bone or a pair of mussel or clam shells. Eyelashes and the hair of the armpits and pubes were allowed to grow naturally. A minor ceremony attended the plucking of a pubescent girl's eyebrows. Thus, when Lena Underwood was about thirteen her parents paid Julia Cole's mother $50 to pluck the girl's eyebrows and apply a secret medicine which was supposed to prevent the hair from growing again. The old lady (a Makah) took dentalium shells and crushed them on a hard black rock from the beach. Then she secured a special kind of rock which had always been under water and boiled it until an “oil” came out. This was mixed with the powdered shell and rubbed on the girl's eyebrows. A pubescent girl would beat rocks together “until they sweat” (until a powder formed). Then she took shredded bark, rubbed it in the powder and applied it to her eyebrows to prevent their growing again. A Mrs. Whaler was famous for her beautiful eyebrows and accordingly nicknamed kamtsom˙a (“good eyebrows”). A youth or a man would ask a girl or woman to trim his eyebrows, while for females the operation was performed by a member of their own sex.

Despite the social acceptability of the Tlingit shaman, which contrasts to the unacceptability of the witch, there were several qualities that set the shaman apart from the layman. One such quality was his appearance, which, with his long, uncombed hair, uncut nails, and distinct costume, was most unlike that of the lay person. Other examples of the shaman’s opposition to social norms include the manufacture and storage of his paraphernalia, the manner by which he was paid, and the treatment of his corpse.

## Southwest and Basin

### Chiricahua Apache

Opler, Morris Edward. 1941. An Apache Life-Way: The Economic, Social, and Religious Institutions of the Chiricahua Indians. 1941, Chicago. University of Chicago Press. p.93.

The attendant now advises the girl: She tells her how to drink water through the tube [of carrizo, suspended from the fringe of the dress on the right side], how to scratch herself with the stick [from a fruit- or nut-bearing tree; the scratcher hangs on the left side of the dress]. She tells the girl that she must not scratch herself with her nails, because, if she does, it will leave scars, and that she must not touch water with her lips but must use the tube for eight days or it will rain. 

### Havasupai

Spier, Leslie. 1928. “Havasupai Ethnography.” In Anthropological Papers of the American Museum of Natural History, v. XXIX. 1928, New York City. The Trustees. 

p.194.

According to informants, hair cuttings are burned so that the birds cannot use them in nest-building, which the natives would not like. But I noted that hair clippings were left strewn about the camps. No care is taken of nail pairings.

p.196.

Red paint is not obtainable near the village, but is taken from a mine on Diamond Creek in Walapai territory. The mine entrance is a small orifice in the face of a cliff, which can only be reached by a ladder. Only one man at a time can enter, crawling flat, dragging a sack under him. The powdered red clay is scooped into the sack, which is held under the arm as he backs out. This is dangerous work, for more than one man has been killed in the crevice. A second mine is located east of Grand View in their own range. Black paint ( mat˘inyádj˘e, black earth) is scraped from a stratum in a trench at Pine Springs, also in Walapai territory. Charcoal is not used. The red and black powders are kept in little buckskin bags, sewed with a running stitch, with a thong bound about the neck. The red powder is sometimes mixed with water so that it can be rolled into a ball and kept in a bag in this form. Powder is scratched from the ball with the thumb nail until a pinch is collected in the palm. Cold grease, preferably deer, is kept in another bag; it will not spoil for a month or so. It is chewed until soft, kneaded with the powder in the hand, and smeared on the face with the fingers. Black paint is not mixed with grease, but a stick, moistened in the mouth, is inserted in the nearly closed neck of the bag. For a white paint ( mat˘ehé'e white (?) earth) the gypsum found in Cataract Canyon is roasted in ashes for half a day. When cool, it is ground to powder, and mixed with water for use. This is always prepared fresh when desired. Sienna paint ( vialt˙aθlívd, mescal—) is the dried juice of roasted mescal (p. 106). The stick or small bundle of yucca fiber used as a brush is rubbed on a lump of this paint wet with saliva.

p.288.

I was told that hair cuttings are burned so that birds would not use them in nest-building, but I noted no care in their disposal. No care is taken of nail-parings. Cushing, however, implies otherwise: 1 1 Cushing, (a), 555. As an evidence of confidence in a newly-made friend, a Ha-va-su-paí will sometimes give to him that whereby, in the native belief, even the giver's life may be taken by sorcery,—a hair, a bit of his skin, or a piece of his finger-nail,—this being an inviolable contract of peace and mutual regard.

Smithson, Carma Lee, and Robert C. Euler. 1964. “Havasupai Religion and Mythology.” In Anthropological Papers, No. 68. no. 68. 1964, Salt Lake City. University of Utah Press. p.14.

The Havasupai had few concepts of preventive medicine. Strips of porcupine skin with the quills attached occasionally were worn on a hat or on the back of the shirt over the shoulder to ward off illness. A sharp piece of obsidian worn as a pendant was thought to be similarly effective. No decoctions were drunk, no physical exercise was indulged in, and no precautionary ceremonies were employed as preventive medicine. No care was taken to hide hair or nail parings nor was any significance attached to them. Babies' hair, however, was not discarded on the ground; should a bird make a nest from it the infant might die.

Smithson, Carma Lee. 1959. “The Havasupai Woman.” In Anthropological Papers, No. 38. no. 38. 1959, Salt Lake City. University of Utah Press. p.72.

In addition to obervance of certain menstrual and childbirth taboos said to keep a woman youthful and attractive, a Havasupai woman should wash her face daily in cold water, rubbing the skin outward from the sides of the nose and upward on the neck, cheeks, and forehead, to prevent wrinkles. This routine is suspiciously reminiscent of advice given in movie magazines, which are popular with Havasupai women. However, an informant added: “I think this is true, because S—'s face is so smooth in her eighties, and she always did that. Your people don't know these things, and they start to wrinkel in their twenties. But look at me, I'm 44 and hardly have any wrinkles. Another thing, during the first four days of your monthly, don't smile very much, because it pulls your face in wrinkles and will leave lines there. We already told you not to eat meat or scratch with your nails at that time, and you shouldn't smoke for those four days. The same rules are for your husband and will keep him young too if he does everything right. We never told your people these things, so they just get old real soon. We're telling you because we want you to keep young like us. These things will make you look real young till in your fifties or sixties.”

### Hopi

Stephen, d., Alexander M., and Elsie Worthington Clews Parsons. 1969. “Hopi Journal of Alexander M. Stephen.” In Columbia University Contributions to Anthropology, v. 23. AMS Press. 

p.401.

Red, pala'chka, is over the body and limbs, except around the loins and mid-thighs, which is covered with white, tü'ma. No finger nail intaglio (hochi'chitota), or other markings on body or limbs. Threaded discs of turquoise are worn as ear pendants and silver earrings are quite common, but no ribbons or fancy cloth innovations are apparent. As usual, faces were rubbed with red (shü'ta) before donning the maskette.

p.476.

Yellow curved snout, base surrounded with spruce. Various modifications of squash emblems on right side. The imitation Fig. 265. Mask of Zuñi Duck kachina parroquet plumes on crown are dyed pigeon feathers. Two erect eagle feathers. (Fig. 265). (Get back of mask with butter-flies.) Necklaces in great profusion. Body and limbs entirely painted with dark purple (akau'o shibu'sh nümchañwû (pl.), chewed sunflower seeds) which is rubbed on with the hands. Finger nail intaglio saltire-wise on front of body ( naho'˘i hazri'wiyüñwû (pl.), cross scratchings) and on back; zigzag (hochi'chita) down legs and arms. (Fig. 266). Blue-green armlet (shakwa' ma'shmi) on each arm, in which several spruce twigs are inserted, armlet half-way between shoulder and elbow; from each, two or more eagle or hawk or turkey wing feathers (ma'shmi añhai'yuwutaka) depend from white cotton strings attached. Gourd rattle of the ordinary oblate spheroid form, but of various decoration, in right hand. In left hand, the whitened willow wand, six or seven feet long, called ñatyü'ñpi (Fig. 267); the two feathers at the tip called kwa'zrü, i. e. kwa'hü shü'rü, eagle tail, being from eagle tail. The prayer-feather is downy eagle (kwabü'hü) from eagle thigh, under wing or under tail. The wand is held vertically in the left hand, the butt on the ground a little in front of the left foot. White kilt girded with the big belt. Gray foxskin at loins, head thrust under girdle, i. e. head of skin thrust downward next the back, between the skin of the personator's back and his kilt. Broad space above knee whitened with kücha'chka. Tortoise rattle at right garter. Below left knee gartered with hank of yarn, most of them blue, some red.

p.531.

The Hüm'is kachina wear a mask and head piece. Spruce at the base of the mask; hawk feathers (kwa'chakwa) at the rear. The parroquet plume is fastened to the tip of the back stick, and the two eagle tail feathers (kwa'zrü) are also there. Many downy eagle feathers. No necklaces, but instead the back hair (a'ña) is wrapped with cotton string and fastened round the neck. The body and limbs are blackened with corn smut, the mark [unknown] [unknown] (nakwachve'˘eta) in finger nail on each side of breast and on the back below each shoulder blade also. There is no great uniformity in these marks. Some have them on the breast only, and a few are not marked at all. A hank of blue yarn is worn as bandoleer over the right shoulder. One or two have red and black or black and white yarn thus, and one wears the tipush [? infant] bandoleer. Blue armlets, mostly of leather, are on each arm, with spruce twigs thrust in stems down, between armlet and arm. Two eagle wing feathers are fastened to the lower edge of the armlet. There is a diversity in this also. Some have only one feather at each armlet. Some have hawk and some dyed pigeon or hen feathers. On the right wrist they wear the cylinder (mü'˘inko'ña) received from N[unavailable]'ka this dawn; on the left wrist, a wrist guard. A white kilt is girt first with a ñwünkwe'wa and then girt over that with a yarn belt. There is a foxskin at the loins, and about ten or twelve spruce boughs, long enough to reach from the loins and almost sweep the ground, are thrust in between the girdle and kilt, stems up. The boughs are fastened to a stout bit of yarn rope, and this rope is tied around the kilt. The legs are blackened, with a hank of blue yarn below left knee, and a tortoise shell rattle below right knee; red moccasins and fringed anklets. They carry a gourd rattle in right hand and a sprig of spruce in left. The female impersonations are with hair in whorls, and wear a maskette which is of leather, except the strip of blue black woolen Hopi cloth at the lower edge. (Fig. 299). Innumerable bunches of feathers, tail of bluebird (chizro'shürü), with three to five prayer-feathers are fastened to this lower strip. A red hair fringe is worn Fig. 299. Female mask, Hüm'is over the face part. There are both the red and blue bordered and the embroidered cotton blankets in the ranks; black dress, and moccasins as usual. They carry the typical notched sticks; no boxes today, all carry gourds, but only one or two are whitened and decorated.

p.925.

The procession is the same (nearly) as that of the Horn and Singers of last November. 1 1 See p. 988. The procession passed along, sideways, facing south to the pillar rock, not halting, but moving quite slowly, passing between the pillar rock and the houses, and out through the passage to Chief kiva court. They did not pass around Chief kiva, but when Sa'l˘iko on the right of the line got even with the Chief kiva hatchway, she countermarched sideways, and the line passed back again, facing north. On reaching Horn kiva, they passed between the hatch and the edge of the cliff, moving around the hatchway and descending. The song continued as they descended. The movement is a short sidelong step, lifting the right foot and bringing it to the ground with a vigorous stamp, accompanying the stamp with a downward thrust of the right hand, holding the corn ear. The gowned women or Singers make no motion. All these gowned ones have the legs and arms washed with the pale sandy mud, and their faces rubbed with the lilac meal. The women Horns have their faces whitened with clay and decorated with finger nail intaglio.

p.1023.

Formerly the Hopi when going on a hare hunt set one eagle feather on the scalp lock, rubbed the body with red ochre, and with white clay drew a white stripe from the foot up the outside of the leg and from the hand up the arm and over the shoulder and down the side of the breast, on each side of the body the same. A streak of red down each cheek from eye to chin, and from under lip to centre of chin, and over these red stripes two straight finger nail lines. Some also added a streak of Ko'honini red horizontally under each eye. They wore a breech cloth girded with string. On reaching the proposed hunting ground, they took off their moccasins and thrust them into the girdle at the loins.
